meta.schema_note: One object per day. `wellness` and `activity` are pulled metrics; `score`+`components` per DAY_SCORE.md; `entry` is the coach's read; `prediction`/`pred_half` is the projected half time. reviewed=false means routine-drafted, not yet human-amended.
meta.scoring: probability-change model (DAY_SCORE.md): score=ΔP(1:20), score_committed=ΔP(1:25) — INDEPENDENT trajectories that diverge (neither always higher); 60=neutral; equal-100 ceilings; magnitude discipline; green-recovery floor; decoupling weighted by run type; Pacific tz
meta.timezone: athlete US Pacific (UTC-8/-7); Intervals stores UTC but start_date_local is Pacific; evening runs cross midnight UTC
meta.prob_model: p_120/p_125 = P(hit goal if raced TODAY at current fitness) per DAY_SCORE.md. Both round to ~0% through base phase BY DESIGN — the live signal is pred_half falling toward the goal lines.
meta.model_version: v8: two-invocation; full-resolution streams + Intervals interval structure; raced-today probability; Pacific tz

days.entry: Two runs joined together, and the average hides it. The first twelve kilometres are the run the plan has been asking for: 6:12 to 6:59 per kilometre at 127-145 bpm, genuinely easy, the longest of the block. For context, on July 5 you ran 12 km at 156 HR and called that easy — same athlete, two weeks later, further and fifteen beats lower. That part is the base arriving and it is worth more to this race than anything else you do. Then kilometres 13 to 16 went 4:51, 4:52, 4:37, 4:27 at 160-165 bpm. Split by moving time, the final third covered 6.26 km at 5:15/km and HR 154 against 6:46 and HR 133 for the first — the last 5 km ran 106 s/km quicker than the body of the run. The prescription was 5:50-6:05/km with a heart-rate ceiling of 148. So: a strong session, and 4:27/km at 160 bpm sixteen kilometres deep is real evidence of fitness, but it was a long run with a tempo finish rather than the easy long run it reads as — and embedded quality on long runs isn't due until mid-August. Also worth knowing for reading the numbers: 42 minutes and 39 seconds of the 2h21m elapsed was spent stopped, which is why an average of 141 bpm looks gentler than the running was.

stream_read._method: Segmented on the three recording gaps in the time channel (211 s / 172 s / 200 s) — those gaps ARE the standing recoveries, so they define the reps. Each rep then split at 1000 m to separate the 5K-pace leg from the mile-pace leg. Autolap kilometres were ignored: they straddle rep boundaries and fabricate a mid-set collapse that did not happen.

stream_read.cooldown: 1.80 km @ 5:23/km, HR 155 (Z3) — the one loose end; a cooldown should sit in Z1–Z2

components.label: Executed the prescription exactly: every 5K-pace leg landed 3:58-4:02 and every mile-pace leg 3:42 → 3:29. Four reps, four clean gear changes.
Progressive across the whole set — 3:55, 3:53, 3:52, 3:48 — with the closing surge getting faster each rep (20, 20, 24, 29 s/km). Negative-split discipline, not fade.

days.entry: 4 x 1 mile off three minutes standing, exactly as prescribed, and executed about as well as this session can be. The watch pauses during the recoveries, so the three gaps in the recording — 211, 172 and 200 seconds — mark the reps precisely: four blocks of 366, 363, 362 and 356 seconds. Split each rep at 1000 m and both halves of the assignment show up cleanly. The 5K-pace legs came in at 4:02, 4:00, 4:00, 3:58 — metronomic, and deliberately 8-10 s/km slower than actual 5K pace, which is the discipline this session tests. The mile-pace legs went 3:42, 3:40, 3:36, 3:29: at mile pace, then progressively through it, closing the final 560 m at 3:29/km. Rep averages fell every time (3:55, 3:53, 3:52, 3:48) and the gear change widened every time (20, 20, 24, 29 s/km). That is a negative-split set most runners don't manage. HR climbing 174 to 180 to 183 to 184, with recovery depth shrinking from 62 beats to 44 across the rests, is simply the price of four hard miles — and a 62-beat drop inside three minutes on the first rest is a strong number. Two caveats, neither a criticism of the session: CTL 27 is a young base to be running mile-pace work on, and mile speed is not the limiter here — endurance is. The one loose end is the cooldown at 155 bpm in Z3, which should sit in Z1-Z2. This also firms up the 5K picture: 4 x 1 mile averaging 3:52 off short rest sits with the critical-speed model's 19:07 rather than December's 19:17 being the ceiling.
